newsitem.title: USA: Florida court hears argument on education.
newsitem.headline: Florida court hears argument on education.

text.p: A group advocating higher public school spending told the Florida Supreme Court Friday the state's constitution should include a guarantee that 40 percent of Florida's budget be spent on education.
Opponents said such a requirement would result in an immediate $1.6 billion adjustment to the state's budget and would unlawfully tie the hands of lawmakers and the governor.
The high court must now decide whether voters will have the opportunity to end the debate.

The court, which heard arguments in the state's 150-year-old capital, will rule on whether the proposal will unduly harm multiple functions of state government or if voters can decide whether the provision is etched into the constitution.
Attorneys for the Coalition to Reclaim Education's Share argued that the state budget requires officials to offer residents an adequate system of public education.
Since 1986, however, the percentage of the state's $42 billion budget spent on education has fallen from 40 percent to about 35 percent, a decline the group says betrays that constitutional mandate.
The coalition has started a petition drive to put the issue to Florida voters.
"If we wait until the legislature to do this at their current rate it would take them 50 years," said Jon Mill, a former House Speaker and now an attorney representing the group.

Amendment opponents, however, told the court to reject the proposed amendment would tie the hands of the governor and lawmakers, who would be required to set aside 40 percent of each budget for education. Secondly, critics say passage of the amendment would set a precedent.

"The question is what if someone comes back next year for the interest and someone the following year (does the same)," said Barry Richard, an attorney representing Citizens for Budget Fairness, a recently assembled group organized to oppose the proposed amendment.
"After a while you don't need a legislature anymore."

To put the issue to voters, the coalition must obtain 429,000 signatures. In addition, the amendment language must be approved by the state supreme court, which determines if the ballot language is accurate and the proposal is geared toward a single subject and will not substantially affect many areas of government.
As is customary, the high court gave no indication when it would rule.
